newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Lehman ring exit highlights LME trade blues.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lehman ring exit highlights LME trade blues.

text.p: A decision by Lehman Brothers Commodities to quit the floor of the London Metal Exchange (LME) is the latest and largest in a series of adjustments on the metals market since the Sumitomo scandal erupted in June.

Other metal companies have cut staff numbers and bonus payments, but Lehman is the first firm to stop trading on the actual market floor, trade sources said. "They are very big fish indeed and it is a worrying sign for the market," a senior trader said. Lehman is a subsidiary of Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc, which said on Wednesday it is to wind down its existing business in metals and energy. Metals and energy employ around 35 staff in London and several have already left, Lehman said.
The company will retain LME clearing member status to service futures business but its exit from the floor cuts the number of LME ring dealers to 16.
"This is a big surprise. Although Lehman were not the force they previously were, they were still doing considerable amounts of business at times," an analyst said.
Activity on the LME, hub of the global trade in metals, has slumped since mid-June when Sumitomo Corp of Japan fired star trader Yasuo Hamanaka.

A key figure in copper, and believed by other traders to have been the mastermind behind a high price trading strategy, Hamanaka was said by Sumitomo to have admitted running up losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading.

A lack of liquidity subsequently pinched the metals trade. "People are doing less business, so commissions are down, but overheads stay the same. It is cyclical to some extent, but still a worry," an industry source said.
Standard Chartered Plc decided this month to merge its LME dealing subsidiary Mocatta Base Metals with Mocatta Bullion, amid some talk that the merged unit would be for sale.
There have been three staff departures from Deutsche Bank Sharps Pixley Metals, as Deutsche Bank AG's banking business in London, Morgan Grenfell, restructures.
LME ring dealer Rudolf Wolff, a subsidiary of Canada's Noranda Inc, restructured its Tokyo operations in October and moved some operations to London.
There may be further changes in coming weeks as well, as Lehman's departure reduces LME liquidity even more.
"Since the copper crisis, there have been lots of people saying that parent companies are looking to sell their ring dealers," the analyst said.
"Some of these brokerage houses are putting up too much risk capital on extended credit lines, for example, and getting very little return," the senior trader said.
Changes are taking place off the market as well, as some of the huge investment houses reduce their metal operations. Perhaps the most notable casualty was Winchester Commodities.
Hit by low volumes, Winchester largely withdrew from the base metals business, amid several redundancies.
But traders say that it is not all doom and gloom in the metals world, with expansions taking place off and on the LME.
Chase Manhattan is expanding its metals risk managment business in New York and London and Standard Bank of London has hired staff this year as it develops in base metals.
Meanwhile, on the LME, FIMAT Metals, which acquired ring dealer Brody White in 1995, is enlarging its metal trading unit.
